summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record.

Access to sex-separated facilities is contested in Paraná's own legislature and councils. In 2021 state representative Mara Lima introduced a bill banning unisex bathrooms statewide and requiring separate male and female facilities; on 16 November 2021 the Curitiba City Council approved a municipal bill of the same kind introduced by councilman Ezequias Barros. On 4 October 2023 the Curitiba City Council passed a protest motion against Resolution 2/2023 of the federal Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, which told educational institutions to guarantee bathroom and changing-room use according to each student's gender identity. The Ministry had stated that the resolution was not binding and obliged no school to adopt it, and the Curitiba vote was symbolic, to be converted into an official letter to the federal government.

Civil registry markers in Paraná have moved in both directions within a two-year span. In 2023 the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of 'non-binary' in the civil registry gender marker, then revoked it in November 2023, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to 'male' and 'female' only. In 2025 the same court authorized a third gender option on documents.

Municipal sport rules in Londrina are the most litigated local restriction. On 26 April 2024 Londrina enacted a law banning transgender people from competing according to gender identity, with a R$10,000 fine for non-compliance. On 26 February 2026 the City Council approved a motion to bar transgender athlete Tiffanny Abreu from the Brazilian Women's Volleyball Cup; the Brazilian Volleyball Confederation filed suit in the Supreme Federal Court and Justice Cármen Lúcia issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing her to compete. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organizations filed suit against the Londrina law in the Supreme Federal Court, and on 7 August 2026 rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin voted to strike the law down.

Same-sex civil marriage has been available across Paraná since 26 March 2013, when the state authorized it in all cartórios under the same procedure and documentation as heterosexual marriage and allowed conversion of a stable union into marriage without judicial authorization. The General Inspector of Justice of Paraná ruled the same day that same-sex marriage and the conversion of stable unions to marriage must use normal marriage procedures.

Curitiba registered what the source describes as the first recognition of a same-sex union in Brazil, in 2004, granting common-law marriage status to an English-Brazilian couple who had cohabited fourteen years, a status previously limited to opposite-sex couples.

Family formation has been tested repeatedly in Paraná's courts. On 14 May 2009 the 2nd Court of Childhood, Youth and Adoption granted the first gay-couple adoption in the state to a Curitiba couple, finding a stable and affectionate union able to raise a child in a healthy environment. On 27 October 2010 Judge Sergio Luiz Kreuz in Cascavel authorized irreversible adoption of an eight-year-old child with cerebral palsy by a gay couple together twelve years, under Superior Court of Justice precedent. On 16 September 2011 Maringá justice authorized adoption of two children by a lesbian couple.
tangentialFactors:
Two strands run in opposite directions inside Paraná. Municipal and state legislative bodies have moved to restrict gender-identity-based access to facilities and sport, while the state's Court of Justice has moved to widen document markers, adding a third gender option in 2025 after withdrawing a non-binary registry provision in 2023.

The Londrina sports dispute has been carried to the national Supreme Federal Court rather than resolved locally, and an injunction has kept the challenged athlete eligible while the case runs. A visitor to Londrina therefore faces a municipal law whose operative effect is suspended by a national court order, with only a rapporteur's vote to strike it down as of 7 August 2026.

The Curitiba protest motion of 4 October 2023 was directed at a federal resolution that its own issuing ministry described as non-binding, so the motion carries symbolic weight rather than legal force for anyone using school facilities in the city.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking a registry marker other than male or female in Paraná deal with a Court of Justice that authorized a third gender option on documents in 2025, after revoking a 2023 non-binary provision in November of that year and limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to 'male' and 'female'.

Same-sex couples in the state have an adoption record going back to the 14 May 2009 Curitiba decision, with further authorizations in Cascavel in 2010 and Maringá in 2011, and same-sex civil marriage has been available statewide since 26 March 2013 without separate procedure or judicial authorization.

Residents of Londrina are exposed to a municipal law of 26 April 2024 that bans transgender competition according to gender identity and carries a R$10,000 fine for non-compliance, and the City Council reaffirmed its position on 26 February 2026 with a motion to bar a named transgender volleyball player from a national cup.

Anyone operating unisex or gender-identified facilities in Curitiba works against a municipal ordinance of 16 November 2021 prohibiting unisex bathrooms, and a statewide bill of the same kind was before the Assembleia Legislativa from 2021.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2021 state bill introduced by Mara Lima was enacted is unresolved in the sources; only its introduction is documented.

No final Supreme Federal Court judgment on the Londrina sports law is sourced. As of 7 August 2026 the record contains rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin's vote to strike the law down and a preliminary injunction of 26 February 2026 permitting the challenged athlete to compete; the outcome of the March 2026 challenge is not sourced.

The scope of the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná's 2025 authorization of a third gender option is unresolved: the sources do not say whether it applies to all registries in the state, to which documents, or under what procedure.

Whether the Curitiba City Council's protest letter of October 2023 was delivered or answered, and whether the municipal unisex-bathroom ordinance of November 2021 remains in force, are not sourced.

The claim that the 2004 Curitiba union recognition was the first in Brazil is stated by the source without corroboration in the inventory.
